corpus_definition: From a faraway and unusual place.

forms.definition: the quality of being unusual and from a faraway place
forms.example: Tourists love the exoticism of the old markets in Bukhara.
forms.note: Not common in everyday speech; people usually say 'it feels exotic'.

syn.note: Related: the quality of being unusual, but not always in a good or exciting way.

forms.note: No common verb. 'Exoticize' exists in academic writing but is not in learner dictionaries.

forms.definition: coming from a faraway country and seeming unusual and exciting
forms.example: She loves trying exotic fruits from different countries.

syn.note: Foreign just means from another country; exotic also means unusual and exciting.
Easy word: different from what is normal, but not always from far away.
From hot, wet parts of the world; many exotic fruits are tropical.
Strange can sound negative; exotic usually sounds positive and exciting.

ant.note: Normal and not special in any way.
Well known to you because you see it often.

forms.definition: in an unusual and exciting way, like something from far away
forms.example: The restaurant was exotically decorated with lamps and carpets from Morocco.

syn.note: In a way that is different from normal, without the idea of far away.

context.text: My aunt brought exotic fruits like mango and papaya home from Thailand. Her kitchen smelled exotically sweet for days, and the whole family wanted to taste them.

reviewer_note: No affix claimed on exotic itself (exot- is not a word); exoticism kept as a formal noun rather than hidden.

corpus_definition: To make something larger in size, amount, or area.

forms.definition: the process of becoming bigger in size, number or area
forms.example: The expansion of the airport will create many new jobs.

syn.note: Easy, common word; growth is more general.
Usually about numbers or amounts, not area.
Development is about becoming bigger AND better or more advanced.

ant.note: Making something smaller or less.

forms.definition: a very large open area of land, water or sky
forms.example: We drove for hours across the wide expanse of the desert.
forms.note: Belongs to expand = spread over a large area, not making something larger. Mostly used in writing.

forms.definition: to make something bigger in size, number or area
forms.example: The business will expand into new cities next year.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; expand is a little more formal.
Usually about numbers and amounts: increase prices, increase sales.
Make something physically bigger, like a photo or a room.
Make longer or bigger, often by adding a part: extend a house.
Make something wider, like a road.

ant.note: Become smaller.
Make something smaller in size or amount.
Become smaller or tighter; a little formal.

forms.definition: growing bigger in size or number
forms.example: Tashkent is a fast expanding city.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
Growing and becoming more advanced.

ant.note: Becoming smaller.

forms.definition: covering a large area; or friendly and happy to talk
forms.example: The hotel has expansive gardens with fountains.
forms.note: Belongs to expand = spread over a wide area, or a person who is open and talkative, not making something larger.

forms.definition: in a friendly way, talking a lot and openly
forms.example: He smiled and talked expansively about his trip to Samarkand.
forms.note: Goes with expansive (friendly and talkative). Not common.

context.text: Our school wants to expand next year. The expansion will add ten new classrooms for the expanding number of students in our district.

reviewer_note: No -ion affix claimed on expansion (removing it leaves expans-, not a word). expanse/expansive kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A person who knows a lot about a particular subject.

forms.definition: a person who knows a lot about a subject or is very good at something
forms.example: He is an expert at fixing old computers.

syn.note: Very close; often used for doctors and scientists.
A person whose knowledge everyone respects.
Someone who does a job for money and with training; not always an expert.
A person who is extremely skilled, often in an art or craft.

ant.note: Someone who is just starting to learn something.
Someone who does something for fun, not as a job.

forms.definition: special skill or knowledge in a particular subject
forms.example: We need someone with expertise in computers.

syn.note: Easy word: the ability to do something well.
What you know; expertise is a high level of it.
Informal: practical knowledge of how to do something.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: having or showing special skill or knowledge
forms.example: She gave us some expert advice about our garden.

syn.note: Good at something because of training or practice.
Good at something because you have done it for a long time.
Done to the high standard of a trained worker.

ant.note: Not done by a professional; sometimes means not very good.
Without special training or skill.

forms.definition: in a very skilful way
forms.example: The chef expertly cut the vegetables in seconds.

syn.note: Same meaning. British spelling: skilfully.
Easy, general word; expertly means very, very well.

ant.note: In a way that is not good or skilful.
In a careless way that often breaks or drops things.

context.text: My uncle is an expert in old cars. He fixed my engine expertly in one hour, and his expertise saved me a lot of money.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); expertise is an extra. Don't confuse expert with experience/experienced (different family).

corpus_definition: to use someone unfairly for your own benefit

forms.definition: unfair treatment of people so that someone else can get money or benefit
forms.example: The report showed the exploitation of children in some factories.

syn.note: Cruel or wrong treatment; stronger and wider in meaning.
Using something in the wrong way, not always unfairly to people.

forms.definition: a brave, exciting or unusual act
forms.example: He told us stories about his exploits in the mountains.
forms.note: Belongs to exploit = a brave adventure (noun, stress on EX-), not using people unfairly. Usually plural: exploits.

forms.definition: to treat someone unfairly to get something for yourself
forms.example: The company exploited its workers with low wages.

syn.note: Very close and common in speech.
Easy word: 'He just uses people.' Use can also be neutral.
Treat badly or cruelly; stronger.
Use something in the wrong way.

forms.definition: treating people unfairly in order to get money or benefit
forms.example: Many people think these low wages are exploitative.

syn.note: Easy word: not right or not equal.

ant.note: Treating people in an equal and right way.

forms.definition: treated unfairly by someone who gets money or benefit from you
forms.example: The exploited workers finally asked for better pay.

forms.note: No common adverb; 'exploitatively' is very rare.

context.text: Some factories exploit young workers by paying them very little. A newspaper wrote about this exploitation, and many people stopped buying clothes from those exploitative companies.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: exploit also means 'use resources well' (exploit oil) and the noun 'brave act'; map keeps the 'use people unfairly' sense.

corpus_definition: to send goods to another country to sell them there

forms.definition: a product that is sold to another country, or the selling of it
forms.example: Cotton is one of Uzbekistan's main exports.
forms.note: Stress changes: the noun is EX-port, the verb is ex-PORT.

syn.note: Things that are made to be sold, inside or outside the country.
The general activity of buying and selling.

ant.note: A product that is brought into a country to sell.

forms.definition: to send goods to another country to sell them there
forms.example: Our country will export more grain this year.
forms.note: In computing it also means to save data in another format.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Send goods, by sea, air or road; not always to sell.
Buy and sell, in both directions.

ant.note: Bring goods into a country to sell them.

forms.note: 'Exportable' exists but is rare. The noun is often used like an adjective: export goods, export market.
No adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person, company or country that sells goods to other countries
people.example: Uzbekistan is a big exporter of dried fruit.

context.text: Uzbekistan exports cotton and fruit to many countries. Cotton is one of its most important exports, and many local exporters send dried apricots to Russia and China.

reviewer_note: Noun/verb stress difference noted. No ex- prefix claimed (ex- is not in the affix table).

corpus_definition: A common group of words used to mean something specific.

forms.definition: a word or group of words with a special meaning
forms.example: That is an interesting expression.
forms.note: Also means the look on someone's face, or showing your feelings; this map is about words.

syn.note: A small group of words; very close.
An expression whose meaning is different from its single words: 'break a leg'.
A well-known sentence with advice or wisdom.
A word or phrase used in a special subject, like medicine or law.

forms.definition: to show what you think or feel with words or actions
forms.example: She expressed her thanks to the teachers.
forms.note: Belongs to expression = showing feelings or ideas, not a fixed group of words.

forms.definition: showing feelings or thoughts very clearly
forms.example: The singer has a very expressive voice.
forms.note: Belongs to expression = showing feelings, not a fixed group of words.

forms.definition: very fast, or sent quickly
forms.example: We took the express train from Tashkent to Samarkand.
forms.note: False friend in the family: express (adjective) = fast, as in express train or express delivery.

forms.definition: in a way that shows feelings clearly
forms.example: She read the poem expressively.
forms.note: Goes with expressive (showing feelings), not a fixed group of words.

forms.definition: clearly and on purpose
forms.example: The sign expressly says no swimming.
forms.note: False friend: expressly means 'clearly' or 'for a special purpose', not 'in an expression'.

context.text: 'Break a leg' is an English expression that means 'good luck'. My teacher writes a new expression on the board every day, and we try to use it in a sentence.

reviewer_note: Only the 'group of words' sense is existing; express/expressive (showing feelings) and express (fast), expressly are other_meaning.

corpus_definition: The size, length, or amount of something.

forms.definition: how big, long or serious something is
forms.example: I know the full extent of the damage.
forms.note: Common phrases: to some extent, to a large extent = partly, mostly.

syn.note: Easy, general word.
How big something is, often a problem or project.
How much: 'to some degree' = 'to some extent'.
How much of something there is.
The limits between which something can change.

forms.definition: extra time, or an extra part added to something
forms.example: My teacher gave me a two-day extension for my essay.
forms.note: Belongs to extend = make longer or add more, not the size of something.

forms.definition: to continue or reach over an area or distance
forms.example: The fields extend all the way to the river.
forms.note: Also means 'make longer': extend a visa.

syn.note: Easy word: 'The desert stretches for miles.'
Go as far as a certain place or point.
Cover a bigger and bigger area.

forms.definition: covering a large area or having a large amount
forms.example: The flood caused extensive damage to homes.

syn.note: Easy, general word for big.
Covering a big area or many things.
Happening in many places or among many people.
Covering many subjects or things.

ant.note: Small in amount or area.
Small and not serious.

forms.definition: in a way that covers a large area or a lot of things
forms.example: She has travelled extensively in Central Asia.

syn.note: Over a large area or among many people.
Easy, informal way to say much or often.

context.text: Doctors are still checking the extent of his injuries after the accident. The storm caused extensive damage, and the floods extended far into the fields.

reviewer_note: extent comes from extend; no -ive affix claimed on extensive (removing it leaves extens-). extension kept as other_meaning (extra time / added part).

corpus_definition: A short story that teaches a moral lesson.

forms.definition: a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson
forms.example: He read a short fable to his children.

syn.note: A short story that teaches a moral or religious lesson, usually about people.
A story, often old or imaginary.
Easy, general word; a fable is a special kind of story.
An old story about famous people or events, maybe partly true.
An old story about gods and heroes.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: extremely good or wonderful
forms.example: We had a fabulous time at the wedding.
forms.note: False friend in the family: fabulous comes from the same old word as fable, but today it means 'wonderful', not 'like a fable'.

forms.definition: very famous and talked about in many stories
forms.example: We visited the fabled city of Samarkand.
forms.note: Belongs to fable = old stories and legends; fabled means very famous, not about a moral lesson.

forms.definition: extremely, used before adjectives like rich
forms.example: His family is fabulously rich.
forms.note: Goes with fabulous (wonderful, extreme), not stories with a lesson.

context.text: My grandmother told us a fable about a fox and a crow. At the end of the fable, she explained the lesson: don't believe people who only say nice things to you.

reviewer_note: fabulous/fabled/fabulously share the root but not the meaning; kept as other_meaning with false-friend notes. No -ous affix claimed.

corpus_definition: To have an argument and stop being friendly with someone.
particle_note: Not separable: 'fall out with someone' (never 'fall someone out with'). Without a person: 'We fell out.' Often with over/about: 'fall out with someone over money'. Past: fell out, fallen out. Noun: a falling-out. Mainly British; Americans also say 'have a falling-out'.

relations.note: Have an angry argument; does not always mean the friendship stops.
Easy, common verb; you can argue and still be friends.
End a romantic relationship, not a friendship or family relationship.
Become friends again after an argument.
Have a friendly relationship with someone. American English: get along with.

context.text: Aziz fell out with his best friend over a small debt. They didn't speak for a month, but now they have made up and laugh about falling out.

reviewer_note: Corpus example 'He did fall out with his brother' uses emphatic do; context uses the normal past 'fell out with'.

forms.definition: the state of being known and talked about by many people
forms.example: He found fame as an actor.

syn.note: The state of being famous, especially in films, music or TV; also means a famous person.
Fame for doing something good.
Being liked by many people, not only known.
Fame and praise for a great success.
What people think about you, good or bad.

ant.note: The state of not being known by people.

forms.note: No verb in this family.

forms.definition: known about by many people
forms.example: Samarkand is famous for its beautiful old buildings.

syn.note: Easy and very close in meaning.
Famous and praised for something good.
Liked by many people; a famous person isn't always popular.

ant.note: Not known by people.

forms.definition: known by many people for a special quality
forms.example: The city is famed for its silk carpets.

forms.definition: well known for something bad
forms.example: The road is infamous for its traffic jams.
forms.note: Belongs to fame = being known for something bad. It is NOT the opposite of famous; the opposite is unknown.

forms.definition: in a way that many people know about
forms.example: The writer famously never gave interviews.
forms.note: Informal phrase: 'get on famously' = be very good friends.

syn.note: In a way that is important or worth noticing.

context.text: Lola wanted fame more than anything. She became famous after her song went viral, but she is famously shy and rarely gives interviews.

reviewer_note: infamous is a trap: in- does not make it the opposite of famous, so it is other_meaning, not an ant. No -ous affix claimed (fame + -ous drops the e).
